titre: Kekulé's snake is an 1890 story, not an 1865 fact
accroche: The dream of the snake biting its own tail is told twenty-five years after the paper on benzene. What the paper puts forward can be checked without any dream.
contenu_vulgarise:
The story goes that Kekulé found the structure of benzene by dreaming of a snake biting its own tail. The image is so good that we forget to ask when it appears, and what it replaces.

## When the snake appears

On March 11, 1890, the German Chemical Society holds a celebration in Kekulé's honor, for the twenty-fifth anniversary of his benzene theory. According to English Wikipedia, it is in the speech he gives there that he tells of finding the ring shape of benzene after a reverie in which a snake seized its own tail. The full account, as quoted by Philip Ball, places the scene in Ghent, by the fireside, among atoms dancing before his eyes. In that same speech, according to the account on the site chemie.de, he also advises learning to dream, and not publishing one's dreams until the waking mind has put them to the test.

The Ghent dream is therefore a memory reported at a celebratory gathering. In *Chemistry in Britain*, Ball remarks that such dream accounts appear late in their authors' lives, which calls for caution. Kekulé also places an earlier reverie, on a London omnibus, at the origin of his chains of carbon atoms. Ball judges the two accounts so close in form that it is hard to believe them independent. The chemist John Wotiz sees an advantage in the dream form: you don't have to supply footnotes for a dream.

## What the 1865 paper puts forward

What is dated is the 1865 proposal: a nucleus of six carbon atoms in a closed chain. Kekulé then notes it with “sausage” formulas, soon abandoned. Its strength lies elsewhere than in the image. If the nucleus's six free affinities are equivalent, the number of possible derivatives can be calculated. The theory predicts three derivatives for compounds of the type C₆H₃X₃ and six for those of the type C₆H₃X₂Y, and the *Encyclopædia Universalis* reports that the predicted derivatives were identified, the predictions being fulfilled exactly.

A prediction of this kind is confirmed or refuted at the lab bench, whatever the chemist's dream.

## The displacement

No one can say with certainty what happened in Ghent. Ball writes that in many cases of this kind one can hardly hope to know today what really happened, and that Kekulé's dream is now part of the mythology of chemistry, whatever one does.

The story nonetheless has an effect. A dream gives the idea a single author and a precise night. Yet Ball recalls that earlier work, that of Josef Loschmidt, may have influenced Kekulé more quietly than he cared to admit. What remains solid is the structure and its verifiable consequences. What remains unverifiable is the night.

repere.texte: On March 11, 1890, the German Chemical Society holds a celebration in Kekulé's honor for the twenty-fifth anniversary of his benzene theory, proposed in 1865.
repere.source: chemie.de, “Jahr der Chemie : Friedrich August Kekulé von Stradonitz”

carte.punch: Kekulé's snake is told in 1890. The paper on benzene dates from 1865.
carte.idee: Kekulé tells his dream of the snake on March 11, 1890, twenty-five years after his benzene theory. That theory stands without a dream: it predicts the number of derivatives, which experiment confirmed. The dream remains unverifiable.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Philip Ball — Chemistry in soft focus
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Six pages on the romanticized stories of chemistry, with excerpts of both of Kekulé's dreams.

quiz.question: What in the 1865 proposal can be checked at the lab bench?
choix: The precise night, in Ghent, when the idea of the ring came to Kekulé in his sleep
The text of the snake dream, which Kekulé had recorded in his 1865 paper
The name of the chemist whose earlier work might have inspired the idea of the ring
The number of derivatives predicted for a nucleus with six equivalent affinities
quiz.explication: If the nucleus's six affinities are equivalent, the number of derivatives can be calculated: three for C6H3X3 and six for C6H3X2Y, confirmed by experiment. Kekulé then notated the nucleus with “sausage” formulas, and the night of the dream cannot be checked.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what occasion does Kekulé first tell the dream of the snake?
choix: At a celebration held in 1890 for the twenty-fifth anniversary of his benzene theory
In his original 1865 paper on benzene
In his first lecture at the University of Ghent in 1858
In a private letter addressed to Josef Loschmidt
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is on March 11, 1890, in the speech he gives at a celebration organized by the German Chemical Society for the twenty-fifth anniversary of his theory, that he tells this dream.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What other dream does Kekulé place at the origin of his work, and where did he supposedly have it?
choix: A dream of crystals, in a Heidelberg laboratory
A dream of chains of carbon atoms, on a London omnibus
A dream of concentric circles, during a boat crossing
A dream of flames, during a failed experiment in Ghent
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kekulé places an earlier reverie on a London omnibus, at the origin of his chains of carbon atoms, an account that Philip Ball judges very close in form to the snake story.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many derivatives does the 1865 theory predict for compounds of the type C6H3X3?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The theory predicts three derivatives for compounds of the type C6H3X3 and six for those of the type C6H3X2Y, predictions that experiment confirmed exactly.
